title: Siblings Without Rivalry
author: Adele Faber and Elaine Mazlish
theme: Brothers and sisters fight less and grow closer when parents accept their hard feelings about each other, treat each child as a unique person instead of keeping score, and teach them to settle their own conflicts.
summary: Adele Faber and Elaine Mazlish wrote this book after their earlier work on talking with children and the parent workshops they led. Its subject is the everyday battle between brothers and sisters, and its message is that parents can do a great deal to lower the heat at home.

The first idea is that children's angry feelings toward a sibling are real and need somewhere to go. When a parent says that a child surely loves the new baby, the resentment does not vanish; it simply goes underground. The authors suggest naming the feeling, letting a child say or draw how much they dislike a brother, while firmly stopping any hurtful action. Feelings are allowed; harming is not.

Next comes comparison. Saying one child is tidier or faster than another, even as praise, plants rivalry. Parents are urged to describe what they see in the child in front of them and leave the sibling out of it.

The authors also question the goal of treating children exactly equally. Identical portions keep children counting. Instead, each child should receive what they need, and feel loved in their own special way rather than the same as everyone else.
Another chapter warns about roles. Labels such as the clever one, the bully or the baby tend to stick, and children start living up to them. Parents can help a child see new possibilities.

When fights break out, the book offers a graded response. Ordinary squabbles can often be ignored. When tempers rise, a parent can acknowledge each child's anger, state each point of view fairly, describe the problem, express confidence that the children can work it out, and step away. Dangerous fights call for separating the children right away. For recurring problems, the family can sit down together to brainstorm solutions.
Cartoons and parents' stories show each skill in action, making the advice feel practical.
takeaway: This week, when your children squabble, resist judging who is right; instead calmly describe each child's side, say you trust them to find a fair solution, and step back.

questions.q: What do the authors recommend when a child expresses strong dislike of a sibling?
options: Insist the child must love their sibling
Punish the child for the feeling
Acknowledge the feeling while stopping any hurtful action
Ignore the comment completely
questions.why: The book holds that feelings should be accepted and named, while hurtful behaviour is firmly stopped.

questions.q: Why do the authors warn against comparing siblings, even favourably?
options: Comparison feeds rivalry between the children
Praise is always harmful to children
Children do not notice comparisons
Comparison only matters for teenagers
questions.why: Any comparison, positive or negative, sets children against each other.

questions.q: What do the authors suggest instead of treating children exactly equally?
options: Give the eldest child the most
Give everything strictly by turns
Let the children divide things themselves every time
Give each child according to their individual needs
questions.why: Exact equality keeps children counting, so the book favours meeting each child's particular needs.

questions.q: What is the risk of casting a child in a role such as 'the bully' or 'the clever one'?
options: It has no lasting effect
The child may start living up to the label
It always improves the child's confidence
It only affects the youngest child
questions.why: Labels tend to stick and shape how children see and behave themselves.

questions.q: How should parents usually respond to ordinary, minor squabbles?
options: Step in immediately and decide who is right
Punish both children equally
Often ignore them and let the children handle it
Send both children to their rooms
questions.why: Normal bickering can often be left alone so children practise resolving it themselves.

questions.q: When a fight becomes physically dangerous, what does the book advise?
options: Separate the children right away
Wait for it to end on its own
Hold a family meeting on the spot
Let the stronger child win
questions.why: Safety comes first, so dangerous fights call for immediate separation.

questions.q: When tempers rise, which step is part of the book's suggested response?
options: Name the child who started it
Take away both children's toys
Tell the children their feelings are silly
Express confidence that the children can find a solution
questions.why: After acknowledging feelings and describing the problem, parents show trust in the children and step back.

questions.q: What tool does the book offer for recurring sibling problems?
options: A reward chart for the better-behaved child
Sitting down together to brainstorm solutions
Strict rules with no discussion
Asking grandparents to decide
questions.why: Problem-solving sessions let the whole family generate and agree on fair ideas.

questions.q: What happens to a child's resentment when parents deny it, according to the authors?
options: It goes underground rather than disappearing
It disappears quickly
It turns into gratitude
It is transferred to the parents only
questions.why: Denied feelings do not vanish; they simply become hidden and may come out in other ways.

questions.q: How do the authors make their advice easy to follow?
options: By relying on detailed statistics
Through strict step-by-step rules only
With cartoons and stories from real parents
By quoting medical research
questions.why: The book uses illustrations and workshop parents' stories to show the skills in action.
